verse.speaker: Seer
verse.setting: How a householder becomes a 'world' for others.
verse.sanskrit: यन्मनुष्यान्वासयते यदेभ्योऽशनं ददाति तेन मनुष्याणामथ यत्पशुभ्यस्तृणोदकं विन्दति तेन पशूनां यदस्य गृहेषु श्वापदा वयाꣳस्या पिपीलिकाभ्य उपजीवन्ति तेन तेषां लोको
verse.line: Feed people, find water for animals; when even ants live off your home, you become a world for them.
verse.translation: By housing people and giving them food, he becomes a world for people. By finding grass and water for animals, he becomes a world for animals. When beasts, birds and even ants live off his house, he becomes a world for them.

verse.scene_line: You stand in your house after long days, and feel the weight of its emptiness.

why: feeding and housing others is what makes a home a world

story.title: Markandeya and the child on the banyan leaf
story.story_hook: The whole world was one dark ocean, and on it floated a single banyan tree with a child asleep on a branch.
story.summary: At the end of an age, the sage Markandeya drifts alone over a flooded world and sees a radiant child on a banyan branch. The child draws him inside his body, where he sees all the worlds, then asks if he has been resting, tired. Narayana explains he showed himself because he saw Markandeya's distress. Markandeya tells the Pandavas that this child is Krishna, sitting with them.
story.lesson: When everything you knew is underwater, you have not been forgotten; you are being held.
story.hook_title: An old sage drifted alone over a drowned world, and found a child asleep on a leaf
story.teaser: An old sage drifted alone over a drowned world, and found a child asleep on a leaf
story.for_you: You let go of timidity and held Ram in your heart. Now you stand in the flood with no shelter left. The one who holds the world sees your exhaustion and offers rest.

verse.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse.sanskrit: आशा नाम नदी मनोरथजला तृष्णातरङ्गाकुला रागग्राहवती वितर्कविहगा धैर्यद्रुमध्वंसिनी । मोहावर्तसुदुस्तरातिगहना प्रोत्तुङ्गचिन्तातटी तस्याः पारगता विशुद्धमनसो नन्दन्ति योगीश्वराः ॥
verse.line: Hope is a river: its water is wishes, its waves are craving, and its high banks are worry.
verse.translation: There is a river called Hope. Its water is wishes, its waves are craving; passions are its crocodiles, doubts its birds; it uproots the trees of courage; its whirlpools of delusion are hard to cross and deep, and its banks of worry tower high. Only great yogis, pure in mind, who reach the far shore, rejoice.
verse.why: We think we are chasing things; really, the chase is using up our lives.

prasang.title: Vairagyashatakam: Censure of craving
prasang.summary: The poet confesses everything he did for money and approval: digging for treasure, flattering kings, forcing laughter. He ends with the famous lines that pleasures consumed us and craving never aged, and hope pictured as a river.
prasang.lesson: We think we are chasing things; really, the chase is using up our lives.

verse.for_you: Craving gnaws through what you build. Now you see hope itself is that river, its high banks the worry that swallowed your years.
verse.try_today: Notice when your mind starts wishing and name the worry rising.
verse.scene_line: You stand on the bank of your own life, watching the current of hope pull away from the shore.

why: The river called Hope (Bhartrihari, Vairagya Shataka 10)

verse.ref: Mahabharata · Vana Parva · Vana: Draupadi and Yudhishthira
verse.speaker: Draupadi
verse.setting: Draupadi argues that waiting on fate is no plan: people must act.
verse.sanskrit: कुर्वतो नार्थसिद्धिर्मे भवतीति ह भारत / निर्वेदो नात्र गन्तव्यो द्वावन्तौ यस्य कर्मणः
verse.line: Don't despair because effort hasn't paid off yet. Every attempt can go either way.
verse.translation: 'I keep working and still don't succeed' is no reason to despair. Every effort can end two ways, in success or not; only by not acting is the outcome certain.
verse.why: Do right for its own sake, then work as if it all depends on you.

prasang.title: Do right without reward, and keep working
prasang.summary: Draupadi questions a world where the good suffer; Yudhishthira answers that he does right because it is right, not for reward. Draupadi replies that effort still matters: fate rewards no one who waits.
prasang.lesson: Do right for its own sake, then work as if it all depends on you.

verse.for_you: Yesterday, grace was a place to rest. Today, the work itself is not in vain, because every effort can end in success or failure. You have given fourteen years to a house and a title. That effort is real. The outcome is not the only measure of what you have done.
verse.try_today: Notice one action today that can end two ways and accept both outcomes.
verse.scene_line: You stand at the edge of a life built from fourteen-hour days and ask what it was for.

why: Weariness at unrewarded work is met by naming both possible ends
Failure is one of two normal outcomes, not a judgement

verse.speaker: Ram
verse.setting: Ram sums up his teaching to his brothers in Ayodhya.
verse.sanskrit: पर हित सरिस धर्म नहिं भाई। पर पीड़ा सम नहिं अधमाई॥ निर्नय सकल पुरान बेद कर। कहेउँ तात जानहिं कोबिद नर ॥
verse.line: No duty equals doing good to others, and nothing is lower than causing others pain.
verse.translation: There is no duty equal to doing good to others, brother, and no baseness equal to causing others pain. This is the verdict of all the scriptures; the wise know it.
verse.why: Do good, feel others' joy as your own, and refuse the pleasure of gossip.

prasang.title: Ram on good people and difficult people
prasang.summary: Bharat asks Ram to explain the difference between good and malicious people. Ram says the good are like sandalwood that perfumes the axe that cuts it; they feel others' sorrow and joy as their own and never speak harshly. The malicious burn at others' success and feast on gossip. No duty equals doing good to others.
prasang.lesson: Do good, feel others' joy as your own, and refuse the pleasure of gossip.

verse.try_today: Notice one small thing you can do for someone else today.

why: others' good as the highest dharma

verse.speaker: Hanuman
verse.setting: Having searched all of Lanka without finding Sita, Hanuman fights off despair.
verse.sanskrit: अनिर्वेदः श्रियो मूलमनिर्वेदः परं सुखम्। भूयस्तत्र विचेष्यामि न यत्र विचयः कृतः॥
verse.line: Refusing to lose heart is the root of success. Look again where you have not yet looked.
verse.translation: Not losing heart is the root of success; not losing heart is the highest happiness. I will search again, in the places I have not yet searched.
verse.why: When you have looked everywhere, look again; giving up costs too much.

prasang.title: Hanuman's search and near despair
prasang.summary: Hanuman searches Lanka all night without finding Sita. He is close to despair, weighing what failure will mean for everyone, then tells himself that refusing to lose heart is the root of success, and searches again.
prasang.story_hook: Hanuman had searched every palace in Lanka by moonlight, and she was nowhere.
prasang.lesson: When you have looked everywhere, look again; giving up costs too much.

verse.for_you: Yesterday, doing good was the highest duty. Today, your own weariness asks where the good went. The house, the car, the title are not the whole of your work.
verse.try_today: Look once more at the room you have already left.
verse.scene_line: You stand in the empty room, and you search again.

why: Lakshmana and Hanuman both set the will to go on against despair, inside scenes of real loss.
perseverance named as the root of success

story.title: Surdas: I have danced enough, Gopal
story.story_hook: 'I have danced enough, Gopal.' Surdas's resignation letter from the show.
story.summary: Surdas looks at his whole life as one long performance on a stage, dressed and made up by his own cravings.
story.lesson: Seen clearly, the life driven by craving is a costume dance; one can ask to stop.
story.teaser: 'I have danced enough, Gopal.' Surdas's resignation letter from the show.
story.for_you: Yesterday you were told not to lose heart. Today you see the whole performance and ask to stop. The house, the car, and the title were just the costume.

understanding.emotion: i'm looking for something deeper to lean on
understanding.bridge: What you are living with is what the texts call searching for what it's all for, and that is where this week begins.
understanding.core_struggle: Nothing is wrong but nothing feels meaningful
understanding.mirror: Nothing is wrong but nothing feels meaningful
understanding.insight: Nothing is exactly wrong, and that's the hard part. You've outgrown the reasons that used to carry you.
understanding.mechanism_label: Searching for what it's all for

situations.label: Nothing is wrong but nothing feels meaningful
I'm burned out and running on empty
I've retired and feel lost
I want to reconnect with my roots
I don't know my purpose
I'm struggling with doubt

queries.hook: The wish to understand what these texts teach, and to find in them something steady to lean on.
queries.diagnose: When life is lived only for what passes, the heart feels empty; meaning is missing when we forget what does not pass.
queries.steady: What passes cannot fill the heart; turning toward what lasts gives each day a quiet purpose.
queries.act: Turn toward what lasts: serve, study, reflect daily, and offer your work to something beyond yourself.
queries.story: A story of a student who came to a teacher with questions and was led, step by step, toward the truth.

understanding.life_context: Working and raising kids. Feels searching; closest to is wrong but nothing feels meaningful" and burned out and running on empty".

plan_v3.first_line: You have the house, the car, the title after ten years of 14-hour days, and still nothing touches this grief drying you up.

verse.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse.setting: From the opening section, 'Censure of Craving': the poet addresses his own craving.
verse.sanskrit: उत्खातं निधिशङ्कया क्षितितलं ध्माता गिरेर्धातवो निस्तीर्णः सरितां पतिर्नृपतयो यत्नेन संतोषिताः । मन्त्राराधनतत्परेण मनसा नीताः श्मशाने निशाः प्राप्तः काणवराटकोऽपि न मया तृष्णे सकामा भव ॥
verse.line: I dug, sailed, flattered kings, chased every scheme, and gained not a broken coin. Enough, craving.
verse.translation: I dug up the earth hoping for treasure, smelted the ores of mountains, crossed the ocean, lord of rivers, worked hard to please kings, spent nights in cremation grounds with my mind fixed on mantras, and I did not get even a broken cowrie. Craving, be satisfied now!
verse.why: We think we are chasing things; really, the chase is using up our lives.

prasang.title: Vairagyashatakam: Censure of craving
prasang.summary: The poet confesses everything he did for money and approval: digging for treasure, flattering kings, forcing laughter. He ends with the famous lines that pleasures consumed us and craving never aged, and hope pictured as a river.
prasang.lesson: We think we are chasing things; really, the chase is using up our lives.

verse.for_you: You have the house, the car, the title, and the hollow feeling. The chasing has cost you something real. Let the empty be enough for today.
verse.try_today: Look at one object you gained and ask what it cost you.
verse.scene_line: You stand in your own house with the title in your hand and nothing to show for it.

why: Years of chasing told in first person
The tired 'enough' at the end

verse.speaker: Ashtavakra
verse.setting: Ashtavakra's 'special instruction' to Janaka on why striving and study do not bring peace.
verse.sanskrit: आयासात्सकलो दुःखी नैनं जानाति कश्चन । अनेनैवोपदेशेन धन्यः प्राप्नोति निर्वृतिम् ॥
verse.line: Everyone suffers from constant straining, and no one notices. Seeing this alone brings peace.
verse.translation: Everyone is miserable from straining after things, and no one realises it. By this single teaching the fortunate one finds peace.
verse.why: Peace isn't another achievement; strain less, and stop expecting escape to fix you.
verse.misuse: Not against effort; against the anxious straining that rides on it.

matched.label: I'm burned out and running on empty

prasang.title: Why striving and study do not bring peace
prasang.summary: Ashtavakra warns that reading scriptures, working or meditating will not bring peace on their own; everyone suffers from straining, and running away from the world doesn't end pain. Even pride in being free is just more suffering.
prasang.lesson: Peace isn't another achievement; strain less, and stop expecting escape to fix you.

verse.for_you: You are tired of the chasing. Everyone suffers from constant straining, and no one notices. Seeing this alone brings peace.
verse.try_today: Notice where you strain today without needing to fix it.
verse.scene_line: You sit in the quiet house and feel the weight of all your effort.

why: Where craving is, the round is (Ashtavakra Gita 10.3)
names the straining itself as the cause of the misery

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the inner happiness of one who sees clearly.
verse.sanskrit: बाह्यस्पर्शेष्वसक्तात्मा विन्दत्यात्मनि यत्सुखम् । स ब्रह्मयोगयुक्तात्मा सुखमक्षयमश्नुते ॥
verse.line: Unhooked from outside pleasures, you find a joy within that doesn't run out.
verse.translation: One whose self is unattached to outer contacts finds the happiness that is in the self. Joined to Brahman by yoga, he enjoys undying happiness.
verse.why: Pleasures that start and end can't hold your happiness; find the joy within.

matched.label: Nothing is wrong but nothing feels meaningful

prasang.title: The yoga of knowledge
prasang.summary: Krishna describes the wise: equal-eyed towards all beings, not elated or crushed, finding joy within, seeing that sense pleasures end in sorrow, and able to withstand desire and anger.
prasang.lesson: Pleasures that start and end can't hold your happiness; find the joy within.

verse.for_you: Yesterday named the strain. Today the Gita offers a joy that does not run out, a happiness found inside you.
verse.try_today: Notice one small moment of peace inside your chest before you check for outside approval.

why: the search turns inward
when outer things stop satisfying, the verse points to a happiness that was never outside

verse.speaker: Pingala (quoted by Bhishma)
verse.setting: Pingala, left waiting all night by a lover who never came, finally lets go and finds peace.
verse.sanskrit: सुखं निराशः स्वपिति नैराश्यं परमं सुखम् / आशामनाशां कृत्वा हि सुखं स्वपिति पिङ्गला
verse.line: Pingala let go of her expectation and slept peacefully. Letting go of expectation is the greatest ease.
verse.translation: The one free of expectation sleeps in peace; freedom from expectation is the highest happiness. Turning hope into no-hope, Pingala sleeps peacefully.
verse.why: Letting go of an expectation can bring the sleep that waiting never will.
verse.misuse: This is about clinging to an outcome, not about giving up hope in life.

prasang.title: Pingala's song: the night she stopped waiting
prasang.summary: Pingala waited all night for a lover who never came. At last she saw that her peace depended on someone else's arrival, let the expectation go, and slept peacefully.
prasang.story_hook: Pingala sat awake listening for footsteps that never came, until she stopped listening.
prasang.lesson: Letting go of an expectation can bring the sleep that waiting never will.

verse.for_you: Today, letting go of expectation brings the highest ease. You have the house, the car, and the title, yet the waiting itself is the ache. Sleep is waiting for nothing. That is where your rest begins.
verse.scene_line: Pingala slept peacefully after letting go of her waiting, and you can too.

why: Dropping the expectation is the ease.
The waiting itself is shown as the pain, and its end as rest

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on simple, wholehearted devotion.
verse.sanskrit: यत्करोषि यदश्नासि यज्जुहोषि ददासि यत् । यत्तपस्यसि कौन्तेय तत्कुरुष्व मदर्पणम् ॥
verse.line: Whatever you do, eat, give or endure, do it as an offering.
verse.translation: Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer, whatever you give, whatever austerity you practise, Kaunteya, do it as an offering to me.
verse.why: Small offerings given with love matter; no one is beyond turning around.

matched.label: I'm burned out and running on empty

prasang.title: The glory of selfless devotion
prasang.summary: A leaf, flower, fruit or water offered with love is accepted. Offer everything you do; the divine hates no one, and even a wrongdoer who turns wholeheartedly is counted good.
prasang.lesson: Small offerings given with love matter; no one is beyond turning around.

verse.for_you: Now you can offer the work itself. Do what you do as an offering.
verse.try_today: Before you begin your next task, offer it silently as your only return.
verse.scene_line: Arjuna offers his every action to Krishna, and you offer your next task without waiting for the reward.

why: work as offering

verse.speaker: Ram
verse.setting: Ram asks Bharat to rule in his place for fourteen years.
verse.sanskrit: जानि तुम्हहि मृदु कहउँ कठोरा। कुसमयँ तात न अनुचित मोरा॥ होहिं कुठायँ सुबंधु सहाए। ओड़िअहिं हाथ असनिहु के धाए ॥
verse.line: In bad times, good siblings are the hands that rise to block the blow.
verse.translation: Knowing you are gentle, I still say something hard; in hard times, brother, it isn't wrong of me. In bad times it is good brothers who help; it is the hands that rise to block a thunderbolt.
verse.why: A good resolution gives each person a role and something to hold on to.

prasang.title: Ram and Bharat settle it
prasang.summary: Ram tells Bharat that keeping their father's word is the duty of both brothers, and that the leader must be like the mouth, taking in only to nourish the whole body. He asks him to rule in his place, knowing it is the harder task. Bharat accepts, asking only for Ram's sandals to keep him going.
prasang.story_hook: Both brothers wanted the other to be king.
prasang.lesson: A good resolution gives each person a role and something to hold on to.

verse.for_you: Now the work feels like nothing. In hard times it is good brothers who help, as hands rise to block a thunderbolt.
verse.try_today: Notice one small act of shielding someone else today.
verse.scene_line: You stand in the house you built, and a brother rises to block the blow.

why: taking the hard share for one's family when times are bad

story.title: Manki's song: desire, I know your root
story.story_hook: Manki put every coin he had into two young oxen, and lost both in a single afternoon.
story.summary: Manki spends all he has on a pair of oxen; both are killed in an accident. In his despair he sees through desire: it is born of his own imagining, and he resolves to forgive insults and stop feeding it. Bhishma adds Janaka's verse on owning nothing.
story.lesson: Desire grows from what we imagine. Stop feeding it, and it fades.
story.teaser: Manki put every coin he had into two young oxen, and lost both in a single afternoon.

plan_v3.path: st.mbh.manki_and_the_two_young_bulls -enacts_in-> nirveda, trishna ; st.mbh.manki_and_the_two_young_bulls -enacts_turn-> santosha, shanti
why: Craving is born of one's own imagining; stop feeding it and it dies at the root.
